analysis.one_liner: Lets poor criminal defendants sue states over systemic denials of counsel.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the final three weeks of the Congress with zero cosponsors, went to the Senate Judiciary Committee, and died without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would write into federal law that poor people facing state criminal charges are entitled to an effective lawyer at every critical stage, including bail hearings, paid for by the state. If a state or county routinely fails to provide that lawyer, defendants could join a federal class action lawsuit seeking a court order to fix the system, and courts could use statistics and national standards as evidence. Courts could also award attorney's fees to plaintiffs who win.
analysis.who_benefits: Poor defendants in state criminal cases, especially in systems with overloaded or underfunded public defender offices, who today may wait in jail for days without seeing a lawyer or plead guilty at bail hearings with no counsel at all. Their families also benefit when courts force states to fix broken defense systems.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Indigent criminal defendants and their families

how_it_helps.text: Declares that every indigent person facing state criminal prosecution is entitled to effective assistance of counsel at all stages, at state expense, even where states delegate the defense function to counties.

Creates a new federal class action remedy when a state or county systematically denies counsel, including delays and denials at bail hearings, and lets structural evidence like statistics and national standards prove the violation.
Allows courts to award prevailing plaintiffs reasonable attorney's fees, plus expert fees, so legal aid organizations and civil rights firms can afford to bring these cases.

analysis.who_pays: State and local governments, which fund indigent defense, would bear the cost of hiring enough competent lawyers to meet the standard and would pay attorney's fees and court judgments when they lose these lawsuits.

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes the obligation on states and political subdivisions at their own expense, with no federal funding attached, so the poorest states with the worst defender systems would face mandates and fee awards they may struggle to pay.

Allowing class actions with statistics-based proof and fee-shifting would generate substantial litigation against state and local governments, and critics of this approach argue courts rather than legislatures would end up designing local defense systems.

The bill sets the 'effective assistance' standard as performance under prevailing professional norms, which goes beyond the existing constitutional test for ineffective counsel and would expand what defendants can sue over.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core promise is one the Constitution already guarantees on paper: a real lawyer for poor people accused of crimes. The bill's value is giving that right teeth through class actions, which matters most in jurisdictions where defendants routinely face bail hearings alone. The cost falls on state and local governments, which the bill deliberately declines to subsidize, so the cheapest path for some jurisdictions would be fixing their defender systems rather than losing in court. The main honest objection is design, not principle: an unfunded mandate aimed at the governments least able to pay it.

outcome.mechanism: Senator Booker introduced it in the Senate's last three weeks and it was referred to the Judiciary Committee, which never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Cory Booker introduced the bill in the Senate on December 13, 2022, three weeks before the Congress ended.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Judiciary Committee the same day; no further action was ever taken.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor.
The bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and it expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State and county governments are better off, since they face no new obligation to fund effective defense for poor defendants and no class action exposure. Poor defendants are no better off; systematic gaps in indigent defense remain governed by the ordinary patchwork of existing law.

for.name: Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and got it referred to the Judiciary Committee; recruited no cosponsors in the three remaining weeks.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing, a markup, or any other action on the bill before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no other senator took a position, so the partisan split is unknown; the bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party.

industries.industry: State and local governments (funders of indigent defense)
industries.note: The bill would make states and counties financially responsible for effective counsel in all criminal cases and expose them to class actions and fee awards. That cost pressure exists to force compliance with a right ordinary people hold, but underfunded local budgets would absorb it with no federal help.

industries.industry: Public defender and civil legal aid organizations
industries.note: The bill would create a new class action cause of action and let winning plaintiffs recover attorney's and expert fees, giving defense organizations and civil rights firms both work and a funding mechanism for systemic reform suits.
